## August 24, 1931 — A Monday in the Depression

You arrived on a Monday in late summer, in the second year of the Great Depression. The word "crisis" had become the permanent condition of the world. Banks were failing, harvests were going unsold, families were moving in search of work that wasn't there. The adults around your cradle had grown up in one era and were watching it dissolve beneath their feet.

---

**On the day you were born, a British government collapsed and immediately reformed.** August 24, 1931 was the day Ramsay MacDonald — Labour Prime Minister and a figure who had spent his life as a voice of the working class — went to Buckingham Palace, resigned, and then accepted King George V's invitation to form a National Government in coalition with the Conservatives. His own party considered it a betrayal of historic proportions; the Labour movement would call him a traitor for decades. The crisis that forced his hand was the global banking catastrophe sweeping through Europe — Britain's finances were bleeding out, and his cabinet had split irreconcilably over whether to cut unemployment benefits to secure an international loan. MacDonald held the government together by changing what the government was. You arrived on the day political loyalty broke under economic pressure.

**Less than four weeks after your birth, Japan began the road to the Second World War.** On September 18, 1931, Japanese officers of the Kwantung Army staged a false-flag explosion on a railway line near Mukden in Manchuria, blamed it on Chinese dissidents, and used it as a pretext to invade. The League of Nations, the international order built on the wreckage of the First World War, debated and deliberated and did nothing effective. The lesson was not lost on other ambitious powers. You were twenty-five days old when the first domino fell toward a war that would kill somewhere between 70 and 85 million people. You were ten years old when it reached you directly.

**The Empire State Building had opened three months before you were born.** On May 1, 1931, the world's tallest building was inaugurated in New York — 102 stories, completed in just 410 days, built by 3,400 workers at the height of the Depression. It stood as a strange artifact of the preceding decade's confidence, finished after the confidence had collapsed, a skyscraper that struggled to find tenants for years and that New Yorkers sardonically nicknamed the "Empty State Building." You were born into the world it symbolized: enormous ambition, sudden ruin, and the uncertain question of what would come next.

**The gold standard — the financial architecture of the modern world — unraveled in the weeks after your birth.** On September 21, 1931, less than a month after you arrived, Britain abandoned the gold standard. Other countries followed. The system that had organized international trade and credit since the nineteenth century was dismantling itself in real time. The economists and statesmen who had built their careers on its permanence had no clear map for what came after. You were born in the interregnum between one world order and the next.

**The Depression was not background noise — it was the texture of everything.** American unemployment was somewhere around sixteen percent in 1931 and still climbing; it would reach nearly twenty-five percent by 1933. Bread lines. Bank runs. Families dispossessed from farms. The Hoover administration continued to insist that recovery was imminent and that direct federal relief would undermine character. Franklin Roosevelt — still Governor of New York when you were born — would not be elected until November 1932. The New Deal that reshaped American government was still more than a year away. You were born into the worst of it, before the response had been invented.

---

**The arc of 95 years.**

You were a child during the Depression, an adolescent during the Second World War, a young adult in the postwar boom that remade the industrialized world. You watched television arrive and become the central nervous system of democratic culture. You were a generation removed from the moon landing when it happened, and old enough to understand what it meant. You watched the Cold War that defined your young adulthood end without the nuclear exchange everyone had been dreading since before you finished school.

In your lifetime: penicillin went from a laboratory curiosity to a global standard of care. Polio was eradicated from most of the world. Commercial aviation went from a novelty to the ordinary way millions of people crossed oceans. The computer went from a room-sized machine operated by specialists to a device in every pocket. The internet reorganized commerce, knowledge, and human connection. Then, in your ninth decade, machines began to reason, write, and generate images — a technological rupture that the engineers building your birth year's Empire State Building could not have conceptualized with any available language.

You were born when the world's tallest structure was finished in 410 days and struggling to find tenants. You have lived to see the permanent transformation of what a human being can build and know and reach.

Ninety-five years from Ramsay MacDonald's crisis Monday to now. The Depression passed. The war passed. The boom came. And kept changing.
